name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A
aliases: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type I

clinicalPearls: The most common inherited neuropathy, typically autosomal dominant and caused by a duplication of the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene on chromosome 17
Onset is usually in the first two decades with slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting producing pes cavus, hammer toes and an inverted-champagne-bottle appearance of the legs
Distal sensory loss, areflexia and frequent foot drop with a high-stepping gait are typical

It is a demyelinating neuropathy: nerve conduction studies show uniformly and markedly slowed motor conduction velocities, classically below the demyelinating range, with relatively preserved amplitudes early on
Palpably enlarged (hypertrophic) peripheral nerves may be found owing to onion-bulb formation from repeated de- and remyelination
Progression is slow and most patients remain ambulant, though foot deformity and balance problems are common
Certain neurotoxic drugs (for example vincristine) should be avoided or used with great caution as they can precipitate severe deterioration
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A is a hereditary demyelinating (type 1) motor and sensory neuropathy caused in most cases by a 1.5 Mb duplication on chromosome 17 that includes PMP22, resulting in overexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22. The gene-dosage excess disrupts the normal formation and maintenance of compact myelin by Schwann cells, leading to repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination and the formation of concentric onion-bulb structures. Slowed and inefficient saltatory conduction, together with secondary axonal loss over time, produces the length-dependent distal weakness, wasting and sensory loss. The reciprocal deletion of the same region causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies demonstrating uniform, marked motor slowing consistent with demyelination
Genetic testing for the PMP22 duplication as the first-line molecular test
Electromyography to assess secondary axonal loss
Clinical examination for pes cavus, distal wasting and palpable nerve hypertrophy
Family history and examination of relatives for autosomal dominant inheritance
Nerve biopsy only in atypical cases, where onion-bulb changes may be seen
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric deterioration suggesting a superimposed acquired (e.g. inflammatory) neuropathy
Exposure to neurotoxic chemotherapy such as vincristine
Marked proximal weakness or prominent sensory ataxia atypical for CMT1A
Respiratory or bulbar symptoms suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The disorder progresses slowly over decades and life expectancy is normal; most affected individuals remain ambulant, though many require orthoses, foot surgery or walking aids and experience meaningful disability from deformity and balance impairment.
pitfalls: Administering vincristine or other neurotoxic agents, which can cause catastrophic worsening
Mistaking treatable chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy for CMT and vice versa
Assuming absent family history excludes the diagnosis, since de novo duplications occur
Attributing foot deformity to orthopaedic causes without recognising the underlying neuropathy
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No disease-modifying therapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy with stretching and low-impact aerobic and strengthening exercise to maintain function
Ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, with podiatry and accommodative footwear
Orthopaedic foot surgery such as tendon transfer or osteotomy for fixed pes cavus and hammer toes
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents, plus occupational therapy and mobility aids
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs, with vincristine strictly contraindicated as it can precipitate acute severe deterioration
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling and family screening, noting that the reciprocal PMP22 deletion causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
